cards.title: Structural characterization of bounded-expansion transductions
cards.formal: For a fixed finite relational signature Σ, characterize the classes C of finite Σ-structures for which there exist a bounded-expansion graph class D and a fixed first-order transduction T with C⊆T(D). The source asks for a combinatorial characterization when output relations may have arity greater than two, extending its completed graph-class characterization. The existential transduction property is defined below, but the requested new structural condition is not specified in the source, so this card is not yet a complete proposition with a fixed acceptance criterion.
cards.why: A structural description for higher-arity relations would extend the theory connecting sparse representations, dense structures and logical tractability beyond ordinary graphs. It must retain information in entire tuples, which cannot be recovered from an adjacency graph alone.
cards.status_note: Read the original and full 2018 models and conclusion, checked the 2020 journal abstract and publication history, and read the 2023 decomposition theorem and its graph-only transduction model. Searched subsequent work without finding a matching unrestricted relational-output characterization. The original target remains a broad characterization request with an unspecified structural answer condition. Journal full text was inaccessible; no exhaustive status survey or independent proof verification is claimed.

cards.definitions: A finite relational signature Σ lists finitely many relation symbols, each with a fixed finite arity. A finite Σ-structure A has a finite universe V(A) and an interpretation Rᴬ⊆V(A)^r for each r-ary symbol R; relations need not be symmetric, irreflexive or binary. The signature is fixed across the class, independently of structure size. First-order formulas use relation symbols, equality, Boolean connectives and quantifiers over individual elements; they do not quantify over sets or relations. A source graph is finite, simple and undirected. An r-shallow minor is formed by selecting pairwise vertex-disjoint connected branch subgraphs, each of radius at most r measured within that subgraph, contracting each to one vertex, and deleting vertices or edges; loops are removed and parallel edges merged. A graph class D has bounded expansion if for every nonnegative integer r there is a finite bound f(r) such that every nonempty r-shallow minor H of every G∈D has 2|E(H)|/|V(H)|≤f(r). No particular growth rate or effective representation of f is stipulated. A transduction uses a fixed finite sequence of the following operations: introduce unary predicates with arbitrarily chosen interpretations; make a fixed finite number of copies of the current universe, retaining the relations in each copy and a relation identifying copies of the same element; define new relations by fixed first-order formulas; restrict the universe by a fixed unary formula; and discard symbols. The source also allows intermediate partial unary functions defined by unique witnesses, which can be represented by their binary graphs. All formulas, numbers of copies and numbers of unary parameters are fixed for T, independently of the input graph. Output elements are retained copied vertices, not arbitrary tuples of input vertices. T(G) is the set of outputs obtained over unary-parameter choices, and T(D) is their union over G∈D, considered up to isomorphism. The quantifiers are ∃D,T ∀A∈C ∃G∈D and parameter choices producing A; no single input structure may receive a separately chosen formula of unbounded length. This is a property of whole classes, with no promise that C is supplied by a finite algorithm. For context, a graph class has bounded shrubdepth if there are constants d,m such that each graph admits a rooted tree with leaves exactly its vertices, all leaves at depth d and colored with m colors, where leaf adjacency is determined by their two colors and their tree distance. It has low shrubdepth covers if for every p≥1 there are constants N,d,m such that every graph in the class has a cover by at most N vertex sets, every set of at most p vertices lies inside one cover member, and each induced cover graph has such a tree model with bounds d,m. The constants may depend on p and the class, not graph size. This definition and the cited equivalence concern graphs; they do not define a decomposition for arbitrary Σ-relations.
cards.answer_criterion: The intended result is a necessary-and-sufficient combinatorial condition for exactly the classes C with the transduction property above, uniformly for fixed finite relational signatures. The proposed condition and its full quantifiers must first be made explicit, then both directions established. A graph-only theorem, changing only the source signature, or renaming the defining transduction property does not supply the requested characterization. No particular relational cover condition is currently certified as the source’s conjecture.

context_blocks.title: Dense structure inherited from sparse graphs
context_blocks.text: A first-order transduction can produce dense outputs from uniformly sparse inputs. The graph theorem characterizes such outputs through low shrubdepth covers, giving structural information without requiring a supplied sparse preimage.

context_blocks.title: The unresolved extension concerns output relations
context_blocks.text: The source notes that allowing bounded-expansion relational structures on the input side does not change the graph-output classes. Its next question instead asks about higher-arity output structures. Passing to a Gaifman graph records which elements co-occur in tuples, but loses the tuples’ relation symbols, positions and other information.

context_blocks.title: Later characterizations still have graph outputs
context_blocks.text: Dreier’s 2023 Theorem 1.6 gives equivalent lacon-, shrub- and parity-decomposition characterizations of structurally bounded expansion. The theorem explicitly quantifies over graph classes, so it is not itself the general relational characterization requested here.

context_blocks.title: Structural and algorithmic questions differ
context_blocks.text: The source connects structural descriptions with first-order model checking, but obtaining an algorithm also requires access to suitable representations or decompositions. An efficient model-checking theorem alone does not specify the missing higher-arity characterization.

cards.context:
A first-order transduction can produce dense outputs from uniformly sparse inputs. The graph theorem characterizes such outputs through low shrubdepth covers, giving structural information without requiring a supplied sparse preimage.

The source notes that allowing bounded-expansion relational structures on the input side does not change the graph-output classes. Its next question instead asks about higher-arity output structures. Passing to a Gaifman graph records which elements co-occur in tuples, but loses the tuples’ relation symbols, positions and other information.

Dreier’s 2023 Theorem 1.6 gives equivalent lacon-, shrub- and parity-decomposition characterizations of structurally bounded expansion. The theorem explicitly quantifies over graph classes, so it is not itself the general relational characterization requested here.

The source connects structural descriptions with first-order model checking, but obtaining an algorithm also requires access to suitable representations or decompositions. An efficient model-checking theorem alone does not specify the missing higher-arity characterization.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
